subject: Medieval History
sub_topic: Aurangzeb — religious policy and Deccan campaigns

concepts.name: Reimposition of Jizya (1679): Context, Scope, and Exceptions
key_dimensions: Historical precedent — why Akbar abolished it and what Aurangzeb's reimposition signified politically vs. theologically
Who was exempted (beggars, clergy, women, children, disabled) — UPSC trap on 'universal' application
Economic vs. religious motivation debate among historians (Satish Chandra vs. traditional view)
Immediate political fallout — Rajput revolts, Jat uprisings, and Hindu merchant protests

concepts.name: Temple Destruction Policy: Selective Nature vs. Blanket Iconoclasm
key_dimensions: Distinction between politically motivated destructions (Keshavdeva at Mathura, Vishwanath at Varanasi) and religiously motivated ones — UPSC trap on generalisation
Aurangzeb's own grants to some Hindu temples — contradictions in policy (e.g., Umananda temple grant)
Comparison with earlier Mughal rulers' temple policies (Akbar's construction vs. Aurangzeb's destruction)
Role of temple destruction as political punishment vs. systematic religious cleansing — historiographical debate

concepts.name: Aurangzeb's Enforcement of Sharia and the Censorship of Music, Art, and Court Culture
key_dimensions: Abolition of Nauroz celebrations, ban on music at court, dismissal of court musicians — contrast with Akbar and Shah Jahan
Appointment of Muhtasibs (moral police) — their role, jurisdiction, and limitations
Impact on Mughal cultural synthesis (Three M's — Music, Miniature painting, Monuments) under decline
UPSC trap: Aurangzeb himself was a skilled veena player — personal practice vs. state policy contradiction

concepts.name: Execution of Guru Tegh Bahadur (1675): Causes, Context, and Consequences
key_dimensions: Immediate cause — refusal to convert and championing Kashmiri Pandits' religious rights
Political dimension — Sikh Guru as a rallying point for anti-Mughal sentiment in Punjab
Consequence: Guru Gobind Singh's transformation of Sikhism into a militarised Khalsa (1699) — direct causal link
Comparison with execution of Guru Arjan Dev under Jahangir — pattern of Mughal-Sikh conflict

concepts.name: Rajput Policy Reversal: From Alliance to Alienation
key_dimensions: Contrast with Akbar's matrimonial alliance strategy — Aurangzeb's refusal to continue the same
Marwar Succession Crisis (1678–79) — Aurangzeb's annexation of Jodhpur and installation of Indra Singh over Ajit Singh
Mewar and Marwar revolts — their military and political significance for Mughal imperial stability
UPSC trap: Not all Rajputs revolted — Amber/Jaipur Rajputs (Mirza Raja Jai Singh, Bishan Singh) remained loyal allies

concepts.name: Jat and Satnamis Uprisings: Social Dimensions of Religious Discontent
key_dimensions: Satnami Revolt (1672) — peasant-religious sect uprising in Narnaul, its swift suppression and significance as a lower-caste assertion
Jat Revolt under Gokula and later Churaman — agrarian grievances combined with religious resentment of jizya
These uprisings as evidence of broader socio-economic alienation, not purely religious conflict
Comparison with Maratha resistance — scale and longevity differences

concepts.name: Aurangzeb's Deccan Policy: Strategic Objectives and Fatal Overextension
key_dimensions: Three-pronged objective: eliminate Bijapur (1686), Golconda (1687), and neutralise the Marathas
Why the Deccan became Aurangzeb's 'ulcer' — Jadunath Sarkar's phrase and its meaning
Overextension thesis — drain on imperial treasury, manpower, and administrative attention from the north
Comparison with Akbar's Deccan policy — cautious annexation vs. Aurangzeb's aggressive subjugation

concepts.name: Annexation of Bijapur (1686) and Golconda (1687): Method and Miscalculation
key_dimensions: Bijapur's weakened state after Ali Adil Shah II — why annexation was 'easy' but strategically counterproductive
Golconda's fall — role of treachery (Abdul Hasan Qutb Shah betrayed by nobles), siege warfare
Elimination of two buffer Sultanates that had checked Maratha expansion — ironic consequence
UPSC trap: Aurangzeb destroyed his own strategic buffer, inadvertently strengthening Maratha territorial ambitions

concepts.name: Shivaji and Aurangzeb: The Agra Episode (1666) and Its Aftermath
key_dimensions: Shivaji's visit to Agra, his humiliation at court, dramatic escape — sequence of events and political significance
Treaty of Purandar (1665) as the diplomatic context — Jai Singh's role as Mughal negotiator
Shivaji's coronation (1674) as a direct response — assertion of Kshatriya legitimacy against Mughal suzerainty
Aurangzeb's underestimation of Maratha resilience — a recurring strategic error

concepts.name: Maratha Guerrilla Warfare (Ganimi Kava) vs. Mughal Imperial Army: Strategic Asymmetry
key_dimensions: Concept of Ganimi Kava — swift raids, scorched earth, avoidance of pitched battle, use of terrain
Why Mughal military model (heavy cavalry, artillery, prolonged sieges) was ill-suited for Deccan warfare
Economic dimension — Maratha plunder of Mughal supply lines and treasury towns
UPSC angle: This asymmetry as a precursor to the collapse of Mughal military supremacy post-Aurangzeb

concepts.name: Aurangzeb's Long Deccan Sojourn (1682–1707): Administrative Consequences
key_dimensions: 25-year absence from the Mughal heartland — impact on central administration and provincial governance
Rise of autonomous nobles and governors (mansabdars acting independently) during his absence
Financial crisis — cost of Deccan campaigns depleted the imperial treasury built by Akbar and Shah Jahan
Comparison: Akbar's personal supervision of administration vs. Aurangzeb's delegation by necessity

concepts.name: Mansabdari System Under Aurangzeb: Structural Strains
key_dimensions: Inflation of mansabs — too many mansabdars, insufficient jagirs (jagirdari crisis)
Aurangzeb's attempt at stricter auditing (dagh and chehra) vs. reality of declining effectiveness
Role of Deccan campaigns in exacerbating the jagir shortage — new territories couldn't compensate for costs
UPSC trap: The jagirdari crisis is often confused as Aurangzeb's creation, but roots lie in Shahjahan's reign — Aurangzeb accelerated it

concepts.name: Zamindari and Peasant Relations Under Aurangzeb: Agrarian Discontent
key_dimensions: Increased revenue demands to fund Deccan wars — burden on peasantry leading to rebellions
Zamindars as intermediaries increasingly resisting Mughal demands — proto-autonomous power centres
Jat, Bundela, and other zamindar-led revolts as agrarian phenomena with religious colour
Comparison with Akbar's land revenue system (Todar Mal's Zabt) — was Aurangzeb's administration as systematic?

concepts.name: Aurangzeb's Succession Wars and Their Long-Term Significance
key_dimensions: War of Succession (1657–58) — Aurangzeb vs. Dara Shikoh, Shah Shuja, Murad — ideological as well as political conflict
Dara Shikoh as the 'road not taken' — his syncretic philosophy (Majma-ul-Bahrain) vs. Aurangzeb's orthodoxy
Imprisonment of Shah Jahan — patricide parallel (though not literal) and legitimacy questions
UPSC trap: Aurangzeb's victory is often oversimplified as 'orthodox Islam winning' — political and military factors were equally decisive

concepts.name: Historiographical Debate: Aurangzeb as Fanatic vs. Pragmatic Emperor
key_dimensions: Traditional view (Jadunath Sarkar) — religious bigotry as primary cause of Mughal decline
Revisionist view (Satish Chandra, Audrey Truschke) — political and fiscal compulsions drove most decisions; religious policy was instrumental
Truschke's argument: Aurangzeb interacted respectfully with Hindu scholars and maintained Hindu officers
UPSC angle: Questions often test whether students can present a balanced, evidence-based view rather than a caricature

concepts.name: Aurangzeb's Administration of the Deccan: Structural Challenges
key_dimensions: Creation of new Deccan subas (Bijapur, Hyderabad) — administrative integration problems
Conflict between Aurangzeb's sons (Muazzam, Azam, Akbar) in Deccan governorships — internal dynastic tensions
Prince Akbar's rebellion and flight to Shivaji/later to Persia — a dramatic case of dynastic fracture
Why Deccan remained ungovernable despite military conquest — societal, geographical, and political reasons

concepts.name: Aurangzeb and the Marathas Post-Shivaji: Sambhaji, Rajaram, and Tarabai
key_dimensions: Capture and execution of Sambhaji (1689) — Aurangzeb's greatest tactical success but strategic pyrrhic victory
How Sambhaji's martyrdom galvanised Maratha resistance rather than ending it — unintended consequence
Rajaram and Tarabai's guerrilla continuation — decentralised Maratha resistance after Sambhaji
UPSC trap: Aurangzeb 'won' every battle in the Deccan but lost the war — distinction between tactical and strategic success

concepts.name: Aurangzeb's Personal Piety and Its Politicisation
key_dimensions: His personal austerity — stitched caps, copied Quran for income — contrast with his political ruthlessness
Whether personal piety translated into state policy or was used selectively for political legitimacy
The 'Alamgir' title — 'Conqueror of the World' — and the contradiction between piety and imperial ambition
UPSC angle: Separating personal religious conduct from state religious policy is a key analytical skill tested

concepts.name: Legacy of Aurangzeb: Mughal Decline and Successor States
key_dimensions: Direct causal link between Deccan overextension and emergence of autonomous successor states (Hyderabad, Bengal, Awadh)
Weakening of central authority as a template for 18th-century political fragmentation
Maratha ascendancy post-1707 as the most direct military-political legacy
UPSC trap: Mughal decline is multi-causal — avoid attributing it solely to Aurangzeb's religious policy; structural, fiscal, and military factors are equally important
